title: Rotate Image
description:
You are given an `n x n` matrix representing an image. Rotate it **90 degrees clockwise, in place**: you must modify the given matrix directly rather than allocating a second `n x n` matrix.

Do not return anything.

examples.explanation: The first column (1,4,7) read bottom-up becomes the first row.

hints: Where does cell (i, j) end up after a clockwise quarter turn? Row i becomes column n-1-i.
A clockwise rotation is the same as transposing the matrix (swap across the main diagonal) and then reversing each row.
Transpose by swapping matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i only, otherwise you swap everything back.
approach:
**Key insight: a 90-degree clockwise rotation decomposes into two reflections that are each trivial to do in place: transpose, then reverse each row.**

After transposing, the element originally at `(i, j)` sits at `(j, i)`. Reversing row `j` moves it to `(j, n-1-i)`, which is exactly where a clockwise rotation sends `(i, j)`. Both steps swap pairs of cells, so no extra matrix is needed.

**Alternative: four-way cycle.** Process the matrix in concentric rings; for each position on the top edge of a ring, rotate the four corresponding cells (top, right, bottom, left) with one temporary. Same complexity, more index arithmetic, and the usual source of off-by-one bugs in interviews. Mention it, but write the transpose version.

**Common mistakes:** transposing over the full square (every pair swapped twice, matrix unchanged); confusing clockwise with counter-clockwise (counter-clockwise = transpose then reverse each column, or reverse rows then transpose); returning a new matrix when the problem demands in place.

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) Rotate 180 or 270 degrees (compose rotations, or reverse rows and columns for 180). (2) Rotate a non-square `m x n` matrix (cannot be done in place in the same buffer; return a new `n x m` matrix). (3) Rotate by an arbitrary angle for real images (interpolation, outside scope but shows you know the limits).
